prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints in credit relationships amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) give a compact, dynamic mechanism in which a financing friction, namely borrowing limited by collateral whose value is itself endogenous, turns a small shock into a large and persistent fluctuation. The mechanism comes from financial contracting, so it is disciplined by an explicit enforcement problem. It is not an ad hoc wedge. It became a foundation of macro-finance, shaped how the 2007-09 crisis and the later policy-model literature were analysed, and has had nearly three decades to be extended, quantified and tested. The attribution is also clean: the originating contribution has two authors, and the proposed set matches it exactly. After reading the openings I keep this as my preferred configuration, but I do not think it is the broadest candidate on the list.
statement.case_against: The empirical case is weaker than the theoretical influence. Direct identification of the original collateral-amplification channel is mixed, and much of the confirming evidence comes from the adjacent financial-accelerator and intermediary literature, not from the Kiyotaki-Moore model itself. The 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig covered banks and financial crises, so the committee may see overlap in theme and in the lineage of financial frictions. Opening support is also narrow: only five members ranked B050, against ten for B015. Narrow support is not a scientific argument, but it suggests the case has to be made more carefully to colleagues who rank it low or not at all.

responses.point: Dreber ranked B050 first and argued that a prize for the foundational collateral mechanism should centre on Kiyotaki and Moore, with the Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator line overlapping the recognition already given in 2022.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name attribution and with the concern about overlap with 2022. I would qualify her confidence on empirical standing, though. The amplification mechanism is theory-led, and I think we should not claim more empirical validation than the literature supports. The justification is conceptual foundation plus influence on models and policy analysis, not decisive direct tests. I also agree with her that the accelerator branch has a separate lineage, so it should not be folded in to widen the case.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B015 first and called the New Keynesian framework the strongest case on the list, citing its durable influence on academic macroeconomics and central-bank practice.
responses.response: I accept that B015 has the broadest practical influence and I ranked it second myself. My reservation is attribution. At least eight names are credited, and Calvo, Taylor and Woodford leave out Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, who did much of the estimation and policy-model work. That makes a three-name citation contestable in a way the Kiyotaki-Moore pairing is not. The framework's performance in 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation is also still debated. I therefore keep B050 first but name B015 as my main alternative, and I would not oppose a B015 outcome if the committee settles the credit question.

responses.point: Boppart ranked B050 second and proposed adding Mark Gertler as a third name, treating the financial accelerator as part of the same credit-cycle story.
responses.response: I see the logic, but I would not add Gertler. The accelerator (Bernanke-Gertler, Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist) is a distinct contribution with a different lineage, and Bernanke, its co-originator, was already honoured in 2022. Crediting Gertler without Bernanke would split that work awkwardly. Boppart himself notes that Gertler also appears under B015, which blurs the allocation across candidates. A two-name award keeps the citation tied to the collateral-constraint mechanism.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranked B036 first, arguing that the task framework and the trade-shock evidence combine a conceptual account with credible identification and large influence on research and public debate.
responses.response: I rank B036 third and agree its empirical quality is high. My reservation is that it bundles two strands, tasks and skill-biased change on one side and the China shock on the other, with partly different authorship, so a three-name set cannot cleanly match the discovery. Acemoglu's overlap on tasks and the continuing debate about the size and persistence of the trade-shock effects also bear on it. I think this is a serious candidate but it needs a sharper definition of the achievement before I would put it ahead of B050.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the collateral-constraint mechanism as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 recognition of banking and financial-crisis work.
How much direct empirical support exists for the original Kiyotaki-Moore amplification channel, as opposed to the adjacent financial-accelerator evidence.
Whether the committee prefers a broader macro-finance award that includes Gertler or Gilchrist, and whether that can be done without diluting attribution.
Whether the attribution problem in B015 can be resolved well enough for it to overtake B050 on breadth of support.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile as requiring recusal. My research field is corporate finance and financial contracting, which is intellectually adjacent to the contracting friction behind B050, but the profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler or Gilchrist. I have long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell, and an adjunct post at Chicago Booth, and I note these only for transparency. I have not adjudicated them.
